title: The axe in the mouth
hook: a person is born with an axe in the mouth and cuts himself with bad speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: grass sorted by kind, people known by what they do. Your line was only by deeds. Did you find one deed behind a label? Today, a deed done with the tongue. Day six hundred five.

Three days ago you heard the four marks of good speech. Today the Sutta Nipata shows the other side, and it does it with a story. A monk named Kokaliya comes to the Buddha with a complaint about two other monks. Not just any two: Sariputta and Moggallana, the Buddha's two chief disciples. They have bad intentions, Kokaliya says. The Buddha answers him three times with the same words. What happens next is hard to hear. Today: the axe in the mouth.
screen: `A COMPLAINT ABOUT TWO MONKS.` → `THE TWO CHIEF DISCIPLES.` → `THE SAME ANSWER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Don't say that, Kokaliya, the Buddha tells him. Have confidence in Sariputta and Moggallana; they are good. Kokaliya repeats the charge. The Buddha repeats the answer. A third time, the same. Kokaliya gets up and leaves. Then, the text says, his body breaks out in boils, small as mustard seeds at first, then growing larger and larger until they burst, and he dies. The text says he is reborn in the hell called Paduma, and describes its torments at length, in the vivid, frightening terms the early texts use for the results of harmful acts. The lesson it draws is in the verses. A person is born, they say, with an axe in the mouth, and the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly. Look at where the blade lands. Not on Sariputta and Moggallana. On Kokaliya. The verses go on: whoever praises someone who deserves blame, or blames someone who deserves praise, gathers bad luck with his own mouth. A loss at dice, they say, is small next to this. Notice, too, what the Buddha did. He didn't argue. He didn't punish. He said the true thing, kindly, three times, and left the choice with Kokaliya.
screen: `DON'T SAY THAT, KOKALIYA.` · `HE REPEATS IT, AND LEAVES.` · `THE BLADE CUTS THE SPEAKER.` · `PRAISING BLAME, BLAMING PRAISE.` · then, large: `THE AXE IN THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your tongue. Sit and settle, lips closed, tongue resting softly. Feel how quiet it is when the axe is still. Now bring to mind one person you're tempted to complain about. Notice the sentence that's ready to go. You don't have to judge it. Just see it, and see who it would cut first. Then let it rest, unspoken, and come back to the breath at the lips. The bell holds the time.
The axe in the mouth. In the Kokaliya Sutta, the image for harmful speech: a blade we're born with that cuts the speaker first. Today's word.
screen: `THE AXE IN THE MOUTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the axe in the mouth. Today, when a sharp word about someone rises, picture the blade, and let one of those words stay home. Day six hundred five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote the axe-in-the-mouth verse when teaching right speech, and lay Buddhists who keep the five precepts include one against false speech.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a monk accuses your two most trusted disciples of bad intentions. what do you do?
options: expel the monk on the spot.
say, three times, don't say that; they are good.
call the two disciples to defend themselves.
fork.reveal: he simply repeats the true thing, kindly, three times. the monk walks out, and the rest of the story follows from his own words.

original.note: Pali kuthari: an axe or hatchet, the blade born in the mouth in Sn 3.10.

trapdoor: what you thought: harsh words hurt the person they're aimed at.
what it means: in the verse the axe cuts the speaker first; bad speech is self-harm.
what a scholar hears: the Kokaliya story appears both as Sn 3.10 and in the Samyutta Nikaya (SN 6.10) and the Anguttara (AN 10.89).

notes: Sn 3.10 paraphrased. The hell description is summarized, not retold; confirm that's acceptable.
Confirm the boils sequence (mustard seed upward) and that the dice comparison is in these verses.
Confirm the parallels at SN 6.10 and AN 10.89 given in the trapdoor.
'Many teachers read those passages as a warning written large' is a general characterization; a Keeper may prefer to state the traditional reading of rebirth more directly.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the teach recast the Paduma hell passage as 'a warning written large' on the authority of unnamed 'many teachers', which softens what the text says; it now reports the text (rebirth in the Paduma hell) without interpreting it away. Cut 'everyone looked up to', 'one of the most sobering stories' and the trapdoor's inference about how widely the story was told; howItsDone no longer puts 'harmful speech' in the precepts (the fourth precept is false speech).
